findings.message: The migration also switches the primary keys of all three tables from AutoField to BigAutoField. The story didn't ask for this, and on a large RateLimitEntry table it may rewrite and lock the table during `migrate`, which would block rate-limited requests. Lines 286-306 add `migrations.AlterField(... name="id", field=models.BigAutoField(...))` for ratelimitconfig, ratelimitcounter and ratelimitentry. 0001_initial.py creates those ids as `models.AutoField`. The change only needed the `AddField` for `data`. The ALTER is there because the migration was generated by makemigrations (header: 'Generated by Django 5.2.1') against apps.py `default_auto_field = "django.db.models.BigAutoField"`, which is unrelated to the bug.

This migration also changes the primary keys of all three tables (RateLimitConfig, RateLimitCounter and RateLimitEntry) from AutoField to BigAutoField. That is unrelated to the token-bucket fix. On PostgreSQL and MySQL it rewrites each table while holding an exclusive lock, and RateLimitEntry can be very large because it stores one row per request for sliding windows. Running `migrate` during an upgrade could block rate-limited traffic for a long time. Nothing in the changelog or upgrade notes mentions this, and the PR describes the change as a simple added column. Split the PK changes into a separate, documented migration (or leave them out) so the fix migration only adds the column. The index renames run only when the installed Django has `RenameIndex`. Installs on Django 3.2 or 4.0, which the project still supports, end up with a different migration state and different database index names. On those versions the model's indexes no longer match migration state, so `makemigrations` would generate a new migration inside the installed package, and any later migration that relies on the new names will break. Line 232 has `RenameIndex = getattr(migrations, "RenameIndex", None)`, and line 243 has `if RenameIndex is not None: rename_operations.extend([...])`. pyproject.toml lists 'Framework :: Django :: 3.2' and '4.0' and requires `Django>=3.2`. The model Meta indexes in models.py are unnamed, so Django derives the new names, which differ from the names in 0001_initial (for example `django_smar_key_24c4a0_idx`).

The RenameIndex operations are only added when the installed Django version has RenameIndex (4.1+). The project also supports Django 3.2 and 4.0, so the result of this migration depends on which Django version applies it. On 3.2/4.0 the index names stay as they were in 0001, while on 4.1+ they are renamed. When those users later upgrade Django, the old names will no longer match the model, and `makemigrations --check` will report pending changes or create unwanted migrations. Shipped migrations should be deterministic. Either drop the renames from this bug-fix migration or give the indexes explicit `name=` values in models.py so they always match. The diff adds no test that database token buckets keep their state across requests. That is the behaviour the change exists to fix, yet the committed checklist marks 'Add or update automated tests' as done. Because the database errors are caught, a regression here would silently let every request through. diff.patch touches no file under tests/. tests/backends/test_database_backend.py has no `token_bucket_check` test, and tests/algorithms/test_token_bucket.py never refers to DatabaseBackend. CHECKLIST_database_backend_fix.md line 15 says `- [x] Add or update automated tests (unit/integration) that expose the bug and verify the fix.` The `except Exception` handler in `token_bucket_check` (lines 205-219) returns `True` (allowed) on any error, including a missing `data` column.

No tests were added for the new persistence logic, even though the checklist says tests were added. `tests/backends/test_database_backend.py` never refers to `data` or `token_bucket`. Specific cases are untested: fractional tokens persisting across calls, the fallback for rows where `data` is NULL (using `count` and `updated_at`), the bucket refilling over time, and `token_bucket_info` reading the stored state. The regression from #24 (a missing `data` column, which made every call fall into the fail-open `except` path) would not be caught if it came back. `get()` now runs stored values back through JSON parsing, so the type can change between `set()` and `get()`. For example, `set(k, "123")` reads back as int 123 and `set(k, "true")` reads back as bool True. `set()` stores `serialize_data(value)`, which returns `str(data)` for str, int and float. `get()` returns `deserialize_data(counter.data)`, and with no expected_type that is `json.loads(data)`. Any string that is valid JSON therefore comes back as a different type.

`get()` now returns the deserialized `data` payload whenever that field is set, instead of `counter.count`. This changes behavior for existing callers. A token-bucket key now returns a dict, not an int. A value written by `set()` as a numeric-looking string (e.g. "123") comes back as an int, because `deserialize_data` tries JSON first. Any algorithm code that used `get()` and expected a count will get a different type. The migration has no tested rollback that keeps data. Reversing it drops the new `data` column and every serialized token-bucket state and `set()` value with it. Reversing BigAutoField to AutoField may fail once ids pass 2^31. The diff has no rollback rehearsal and no declared breaking-change path. The operations are a plain `AddField` (its reverse is RemoveField, so the column contents are lost) and `AlterField` to BigAutoField (its reverse narrows to int). There is no `RunPython` or state-preserving reverse, and the diff adds no test of the migration in either direction. The risk.json review focus asks: 'does the down path restore data, not just schema; is the rollback rehearsed?'

The root cause of #24 was that every exception is caught and the request is allowed. A missing column raised a DB error, which was logged and then the request was allowed with a full bucket, so rate limiting silently stopped working. This PR fixes the schema but leaves that path unchanged. Users who upgrade and forget to run the migration will again silently have no rate limiting. At minimum, schema errors (e.g. ProgrammingError/OperationalError) should be raised or reported clearly, not treated as fail-open. `token_bucket_check` and `token_bucket_info` contain the same block for parsing stored bucket state, so a fix to one can easily miss the other. Lines 117-126 and 242-249 repeat the same sequence: `deserialize_data(counter.data, dict) if counter.data else {}`, the isinstance-dict guard, `float(bucket_data.get("tokens", counter.count))` and `float(bucket_data.get("last_refill", counter.updated_at.timestamp()))`. The two copies are not in a shared helper.
